title: How a new AI model could help crushed rock fight climate change - Source
summary: Microsoft and Terradot are developing an AI model that could help make carbon removal using crushed rock easier and less expensive.
body_markdown:
# **The innovation**


Munukutla had worked on AI research at Stanford before co-founding Terradot and had always seen the technology as key to the company’s mission of expanding carbon removal.


While visiting a chocolate maker on Hawaii’s Big Island in 2024, he came across a display explaining how tropical soils are “fast-forwards” of soils elsewhere because the warm, wet climate accelerates natural weathering. That brought to mind Microsoft’s Aurora, an AI model introduced that year and trained on more than a million hours of atmospheric data to predict weather and other environmental conditions. Could it also be used to understand complex geochemical processes?


“We’ve seen AI models develop new abilities as they learn from more data,” Munukutla says. “My intuition was that Aurora could do the same.”


An early investor in Terradot, the Microsoft Climate Innovation Fund recognized the potential for enhanced rock weathering to remove large amounts of carbon. Looking for ways to speed up progress, the Fund worked with Terradot and experts across Microsoft to pursue the idea.


“We went for a moonshot together,” says Erika Basham, director of natural capital investments with the Microsoft Climate Innovation Fund. “We wanted to do more than invest in and purchase from Terradot. We wanted to help solve a problem holding back its growth, and by extension, the industry’s growth.”


The TerraNova model now analyzes factors including the soil composition of a field, minerals in crushed rock from nearby quarries, regional humidity, rainfall, temperatures and global weather patterns such as La Niña to predict carbon removal under different conditions.


That helps it identify locations where the process is likely to be most effective. For example, training TerraNova on data from fields in Brazil enabled it to make predictions for fields in Mississippi, says Oviedo.
